title: The Man Who Sang an Odyssey

lines.text: In 1935, an illiterate singer dictated an Odyssey-length epic.
Avdo Međedović sat down with visiting scholars in what is now Montenegro.
lines.say: Ahv-doh Meh-jeh-doh-vitch sat down with visiting scholars in what is now Montenegro.

lines.text: Over several days, he dictated one song of more than 12,000 lines.
lines.say: Over several days, he dictated one song of more than twelve thousand lines.

lines.text: He had learned it by hearing a friend read a printed version aloud.
That text was about 2,160 lines. His song was more than five times as long.
lines.say: That text was about two thousand one hundred and sixty lines. His song was more than five times as long.

lines.text: Listening was Milman Parry, a young American classicist.
He argued that Homer's stock phrases were chosen to fit the metre, not the moment.
Homer's ships are swift, as Parry put it, 'even when drawn up on land.'
Avdo did not recite a fixed text. He composed as he sang, from ready-made phrases and familiar scenes.
lines.say: Ahv-doh did not recite a fixed text. He composed as he sang, from ready-made phrases and familiar scenes.

lines.text: The story held steady. The words changed.
It has a name: oral-formulaic composition.
In many places still, a great poem is made afresh each time it is sung.

caption: A singer who could not read turned a 2,160-line printed tale into a song of more than 12,000 lines, and showed how oral-formulaic composition works. A true story, fact-checked. Curiouser No. 11
